title: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
summary: Run thousands of LLM calls fast without tripping provider limits: bounded concurrency with asyncio, token buckets, backoff with jitter, response and prompt caching, batch jobs and idempotent pipelines.
outcomes: Explain why a sequential loop is too slow and an unbounded gather is too fast, and size a semaphore from latency and a rate limit
Trace a token bucket admitting, throttling and refilling, and contrast rejecting with waiting on the client
Write a retry loop that honors Retry-After and otherwise uses capped exponential backoff with full jitter
Compute how cache hit rate changes cost and mean latency, and design a normalized cache key
Choose between real-time calls and asynchronous batch jobs, and make a pipeline safe to re-run

lessons.title: Why a plain loop is too slow and a plain gather is too fast

blocks.md:
Suppose you must label 1,000 support tickets with an LLM, using the structured output prompts from the prerequisite course. Each call spends almost all of its time waiting: the request travels to the provider, the model generates tokens, the response travels back. Your program does a few milliseconds of work per call and then sits idle.

A plain `for` loop that awaits each call in turn wastes that idle time. With a mean latency of about 1.68 s (the six simulated calls below), 1,000 calls take about 1,683 s, roughly 28 minutes.

The opposite mistake is to fire all 1,000 at once with `asyncio.gather`. `gather` runs every awaitable concurrently and returns results in the same order as the inputs. Nothing limits how many are in flight, so the provider sees a sudden spike, rejects most of it with HTTP **429 Too Many Requests**, and you pay for the rejected attempts in wasted time and retries.

What you want is **bounded concurrency**: keep a fixed number $C$ of requests in flight, starting a new one as soon as one finishes.

The standard tool is `asyncio.Semaphore`. The Python docs describe it as an internal counter: `acquire()` decrements it, `release()` increments it, and when `acquire()` finds the counter at zero it blocks until some other task releases. Writing `async with sem:` acquires on entry and releases on exit, even if the body raises.

Create one task per item, but put the semaphore *inside* the task around the API call. All tasks exist, yet only $C$ of them are past the gate at any moment.

blocks.title: Six calls: one at a time versus a semaphore of 3

scenes.caption: Sequential loop: each call waits for the previous one. Latencies 1.6, 1.3, 2.3, 1.1, 2.1 and 1.7 s add up to 10.1 s, and the CPU is idle almost the whole time.
Semaphore(3): calls 1 to 3 acquire the three permits at t = 0. Calls 4 to 6 are already created as tasks but block in acquire because the counter is zero.
At 1.3 s call 2 finishes and releases its permit, so call 4 starts in that slot. A permit is handed over the moment one frees up.
Call 1 frees a slot at 1.6 s (call 5 starts) and call 3 at 2.3 s (call 6 starts). Everything is done at 4.0 s instead of 10.1 s, and never more than 3 requests were in flight.

blocks.code:
import asyncio

sem = asyncio.Semaphore(3)          # at most 3 calls in flight

async def label(client, ticket):
    async with sem:                  # acquire, release on exit
        async with asyncio.timeout(60):   # Python 3.11+
            return await client.classify(ticket)

async def label_all(client, tickets):
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        tasks = [tg.create_task(label(client, t)) for t in tickets]
    return [t.result() for t in tasks]   # same order as tickets
blocks.caption: client.classify stands in for your SDK call. TaskGroup and asyncio.timeout were added in Python 3.11.

blocks.md: Two details in that code matter. `asyncio.timeout(60)` cancels the call if it takes too long and raises `TimeoutError` outside the block, so one hung connection cannot hold a permit forever. `asyncio.TaskGroup` (Python 3.11) awaits every task when the block exits; if one task raises, the docs say the remaining tasks are cancelled and the errors surface together as an `ExceptionGroup`.

`gather` does not cancel siblings on failure. With the default `return_exceptions=False`, the first exception propagates to the caller but the docs state the other awaitables "won't be cancelled and will continue to run". If you want per-item errors without losing the batch, pass `return_exceptions=True` and inspect each result; if one failure should stop everything, use a `TaskGroup`.
How large should $C$ be? **Little's law** from queueing theory says that in steady state, throughput equals the number in flight divided by the time each spends in the system:

blocks.caption: C is concurrency, L-bar is mean latency in seconds. Requests per minute is one of several limits; the next lesson adds token limits.

blocks.md: With $\bar L = 1.68$ s and $C = 20$, throughput is about 11.9 requests per second (about 713 per minute) and 1,000 calls take about 84 s instead of 28 minutes. If your allowed rate were an illustrative 600 requests per minute, $C$ should stay near 16 or 17; a bigger semaphore only produces 429s faster.

A semaphore limits **how many** requests are in flight, not **how fast** they start. Concurrency times the inverse of latency gives your request rate, so when latency drops (short prompts, cache hits) the same semaphore sends requests faster. Pair it with a rate limiter, covered next.

blocks.question: You wrap 5,000 calls in `asyncio.gather(*[call(x) for x in items])` with no semaphore. Call 37 raises an exception after 0.4 s. What happens to the other calls?
options: They keep running in the background; gather re-raises the first exception to the awaiting code
All other calls are cancelled immediately and an ExceptionGroup is raised
gather waits for every call to finish, then raises the first exception
The event loop stops and the program exits
blocks.explain: With return_exceptions=False, gather propagates the first exception immediately, and the Python docs say the other awaitables are not cancelled. They continue, so you can lose their results and still be throttled by them. Cancelling siblings and raising an ExceptionGroup is TaskGroup behavior.

blocks.question: Your semaphore is 20 and mean latency is 2.0 s, giving about 600 requests per minute. You add a response cache and 60% of calls now return in 5 ms. What happens to the request rate seen by the provider if you keep the semaphore at 20?
options: It drops to 40% of before, because 60% of calls never reach the provider
It stays about the same; the 20 permits now cycle mostly through slow misses, so misses still go out at roughly 20 per 2 s
It doubles, because the semaphore is released faster
It becomes unpredictable, because cache hits hold permits
blocks.explain: Hits take 5 ms, so their permits free up almost immediately and are reused by misses. In steady state nearly all 20 permits are held by misses, which still arrive at about C / L = 10 per second. The semaphore caps in-flight work, not rate, so the provider sees about the same rate while total throughput rises. Check the cache before acquiring the semaphore so hits do not consume permits at all.

lessons.title: Rate limits as token buckets: RPM, token limits and headers

blocks.md:
Providers limit how much you can send. Both Anthropic and OpenAI measure **requests per minute** (RPM) and **tokens per minute**. Anthropic splits tokens into input tokens per minute (ITPM) and output tokens per minute (OTPM), per model class; OpenAI documents TPM plus daily limits (RPD, TPD) and others. Limits depend on your account tier and change over time, so read your current values from the console or the response headers rather than hard-coding them.

Exceeding any one of these limits returns **429**, which RFC 6585 defines as "the user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time".

A per-minute limit does not mean "anything goes within the minute". Anthropic's docs say the API uses the **token bucket** algorithm, so capacity is "continuously replenished up to your maximum limit, rather than being reset at fixed intervals", and they warn that 60 RPM might be enforced as 1 request per second, so a short burst can be rejected.

A token bucket has two parameters: a refill rate $r$ (tokens per second) and a capacity $b$. Tokens drip in at rate $r$ and overflow is discarded. A request that needs $n$ tokens is admitted only if at least $n$ are present, and then they are removed.

blocks.title: Token bucket: capacity 5, refill 1 token per second

scenes.caption: The bucket starts full with 5 tokens. Each request must take one token. Twelve requests will arrive: 8 at t = 0, 3 at t = 2 s, 1 at t = 4.5 s.
t = 0: a burst of 8. Requests 1 to 5 each take a token and are admitted, emptying the bucket. Requests 6 to 8 find no token and are rejected with 429.
Between 0 and 2 s the bucket refills continuously at 1 token per second, so it holds 2 tokens. Capacity is replenished smoothly, not reset at the top of each minute.
t = 2 s: 3 requests arrive. Two take the 2 tokens; request 11 is rejected. Even a modest burst fails when the bucket has not had time to refill.
t = 4.5 s: 2.5 seconds of refill gave 2.5 tokens. Request 12 takes one and 1.5 remain. Result: 8 admitted, 4 rejected.
Same arrivals with a client-side limiter that waits for a token instead of sending. Start times in seconds: all 12 succeed, the last starts at 7.0 s, and the provider never sees a 429.

blocks.caption: Over any window of length t, a bucket that starts full admits at most its capacity b plus r t. The capacity is the burst allowance; r is the long-run rate.

blocks.title: Burst allowance: maximum admitted requests over time

x.label: seconds since the bucket was full

scenes.caption: With b = 5 and r = 1, you can send 5 immediately, then one per second. The gap between the curves is the burst the bucket absorbs.
A larger capacity allows a bigger initial burst but the same long-run slope. Over a long job, only r matters.

blocks.md: The **leaky bucket** is the mirror image. Used as a meter, each request pours fluid into a bucket that drains at a constant rate and a request that would overflow is non-conforming; implemented with the same parameters this is equivalent to a token bucket. Used as a **queue**, requests wait in the bucket and leave at a fixed rate, which smooths output completely. The client-side limiter in the last scene above behaves like that queue: it delays instead of rejecting.

Token limits are buckets too, but a request draws many tokens at once. The providers count differently, and the details matter:

- Anthropic: OTPM counts output tokens actually generated, and the docs say `max_tokens` does not factor into OTPM. For most models only uncached input tokens count toward ITPM, so prompt caching raises effective throughput.
- OpenAI: the limit is based on the larger of `max_tokens` and an estimate from the request size, so an inflated `max_tokens` reserves capacity you never use. Failed requests also count toward the per-minute limit.

Both providers return headers you can use to steer a client-side limiter. Anthropic sends `anthropic-ratelimit-requests-remaining`, `anthropic-ratelimit-input-tokens-remaining` and matching `-limit` and `-reset` headers (reset is an RFC 3339 time). OpenAI sends `x-ratelimit-remaining-requests`, `x-ratelimit-remaining-tokens` and `x-ratelimit-reset-*`. A 429 may also carry `retry-after`, the subject of the next lesson.

Do not cache or replay a 429 as if it were an answer. RFC 6585 says responses with status 429 "MUST NOT be stored by a cache". Also note that a 429 is not always temporary: Anthropic returns 429 without a `retry-after` header when an organization reaches its monthly spend cap, and retrying keeps failing until access resumes.

blocks.prompt: Your job sends 1,000 short requests. It is far below your token limits, and you run a client-side token bucket set exactly to your RPM. Yet you still see occasional 429s. Name two plausible reasons.
blocks.reveal: Several things outside your bucket draw on the same server-side bucket. Other processes or workers sharing the organization or workspace limit consume tokens you do not see. Your SDK may be retrying on its own (the Anthropic SDK retries twice by default), so one logical call can be several requests. Anthropic also documents **acceleration limits** that can return 429 after a sharp increase in usage, and recommends ramping traffic up gradually. Finally, if your bucket starts full while the server bucket is partly drained, your first burst can overshoot. Running slightly below the limit and reading the remaining-headers helps.

blocks.question: An API allows 60 requests per minute using a token bucket with a small capacity. At 12:00:00 you send 60 requests at once. What is the most likely outcome?
options: All 60 succeed because the minute has just started
About half succeed because limits are checked every 30 seconds
A few succeed (up to the bucket capacity) and the rest get 429, even though you sent only 60 in that minute
None succeed because bursts are always rejected
blocks.explain: A token bucket does not reset at the top of the minute. It holds at most b tokens and refills at 1 per second here. A burst larger than b is rejected beyond the capacity. Anthropic explicitly notes that 60 RPM may be enforced as 1 request per second.

blocks.question: On OpenAI you set `max_tokens` to a very large value "just in case", though responses average 200 tokens. What is the rate-limit effect?
options: None, only generated tokens are counted
Each request is counted against the token limit using the larger of max_tokens and the estimated size, so you hit TPM much sooner than your real usage implies
The request is rejected with 400 because max_tokens exceeds the response
Output becomes slower but the limit is unaffected
blocks.explain: OpenAI's rate-limit guide says the limit is based on the larger of max_tokens and the token count estimated from the request, and advises setting max_tokens close to the expected size. Anthropic documents the opposite for OTPM: max_tokens is not counted, only generated tokens.

lessons.title: Retries that do not stampede: backoff, jitter and Retry-After

blocks.md:
A 429, a 5xx server error or a timeout is often temporary, so retrying is the right reaction. The question is **when**. Retrying immediately adds load exactly when the server is saturated. Retrying after a fixed delay is not much better: if many clients failed at the same moment, they all come back at the same moment.

That synchronized return is a **thundering herd**. It is common with LLM jobs because a single batch run starts hundreds of identical workers at once.

**Retry-After** first. RFC 9110 defines this header as telling the client how long to wait before a follow-up request, as either an HTTP-date or a number of seconds (`Retry-After: 120` means 2 minutes). RFC 6585 says a 429 "MAY include" it. Anthropic's docs say to wait that many seconds when the header is present, and OpenAI's guide treats it as a minimum wait and suggests adding a small random delay on top.

When there is no header, use **capped exponential backoff**. Marc Brooker's AWS Architecture Blog post defines it as:

blocks.caption: Plain capped exponential backoff, from the AWS post. It spaces retries out but every client that failed together computes the same sleep.

blocks.md:
The fix is **jitter**: add randomness so that clients spread out. The AWS post compares three versions, with `random_between(a, b)` meaning a uniform draw:

- **Full jitter**: sleep = random_between(0, min(cap, base x 2^attempt)).
- **Equal jitter**: temp = min(cap, base x 2^attempt); sleep = temp / 2 + random_between(0, temp / 2).
- **Decorrelated jitter**: sleep = min(cap, random_between(base, previous sleep x 3)).

blocks.title: Backoff ceiling and the mean sleep of each scheme

scenes.caption: With base 0.1 s and cap 6.4 s the ceiling doubles until attempt 6, then stays flat. Full jitter waits half the ceiling on average, equal jitter three quarters.
A lower cap bounds the worst wait. Without jitter, every client still sleeps the exact same amount, so the cap alone cannot break up a herd.

blocks.prompt: 100 clients hit a server that admits 10 requests per 100 ms window, and all fail at t = 0. With plain exponential backoff (base 0.1 s, cap 6.4 s, no jitter), how many total calls do they make before all succeed, and roughly how long does it take?
blocks.reveal: Every failed client sleeps the same amount, so the 90 losers come back together at 0.1 s, the 80 losers at 0.3 s, and so on: 10 succeed per round. That is 100 + 90 + 80 + ... + 10 = **550 calls** over 10 rounds. Because the sleeps reach the 6.4 s cap, the last round lands at 25.5 s and the job finishes at **25.6 s**, though the server could have served everyone in 1 s.

blocks.title: Arrivals per 100 ms window (server admits 10 per window)

scenes.caption: No jitter: 100 clients fail at t = 0 and all sleep exactly 0.1, 0.2, 0.4 s. They return together, 90 then 80 then 70, and each time only 10 fit. The herd stays a herd.
Full jitter: each client sleeps a random time in [0, ceiling]. Early retries still collide (some land in the same window), but the load spreads out and quickly falls toward the capacity of 10.
Equal jitter keeps half the ceiling fixed and randomizes the other half, so retries still clump in bands (note the empty windows at 0.3 and 0.7 s).
Decorrelated jitter draws each sleep from [base, 3 x previous sleep], capped. Its first retries already spread over several windows.

blocks.title: Same herd, mean of 50 seeds: total calls and time to finish

scenes.caption: Total calls including retries for 100 clients (100 is the minimum). No jitter makes 550, every client retrying in lockstep. Simplified model: one 100 ms fixed window admitting 10 calls, base 0.1 s, cap 6.4 s.

Seconds until the last client succeeds. Capacity is 100 per second, so 1.0 s is the floor. No jitter takes 25.6 s because the sleeps grow to the cap while 10 clients at a time drain; jittered schemes finish in about 2 s.

blocks.md: In this simplified model (a fixed-window limiter, not the AWS post's optimistic-concurrency simulation), all three jittered schemes cut calls by a quarter to a half and finish more than ten times sooner. The AWS post found that full and equal jitter did similar work, equal jitter took noticeably longer, and full versus decorrelated was a close call. The exact ranking depends on the workload; the robust conclusion is **always add jitter**.

blocks.title: One client retrying: backoff, then Retry-After

scenes.caption: Attempt 0 gets a 429 with no retry-after header, so the client falls back to backoff.
Ceiling is min(6.4, 0.1 x 2^0) = 0.1 s. Full jitter picks a uniform sleep in [0, 0.1]: this draw is 0.024 s.
Attempt 1 fails again. The ceiling doubles to 0.2 s and the draw is 0.109 s. The ceiling grows exponentially; the actual sleep is random below it.
Attempt 2: the 429 now carries retry-after: 3. The server knows when capacity returns, so the client waits 3 s plus a small random 0.311 s so that clients told the same number do not return in sync.
Attempt 3 succeeds and is returned. Total waiting was 0.024 + 0.109 + 3.311 = 3.444 s. If all 6 attempts had failed, the loop would stop and raise instead of retrying forever.

blocks.md: Retry with: honor Retry-After when present (plus a little randomness); otherwise capped exponential backoff with full jitter; a maximum number of attempts and a total time budget; and retries only for retryable errors (429, 5xx, timeouts), never for 400-class mistakes, billing or quota errors.

Retries nest and multiply. The Anthropic SDK already retries transient failures twice by default with exponential backoff and honors retry-after; OpenAI's guide warns that if you retry yourself, you should disable SDK retries or account for them. Three layers of 3 retries is up to 64 requests for one logical call.

blocks.question: A 429 arrives with `Retry-After: 30`. Your backoff ceiling for this attempt would be 0.8 s. What should the client do?
options: Sleep a random time in [0, 0.8] s, since full jitter is best
Sleep 0.8 s, then 30 s if the next attempt fails
Wait at least 30 s, with a little added randomness, before retrying
Ignore the header; it is only used with 503
blocks.explain: Retry-After is the server telling you when capacity will be back. RFC 6585 allows it on 429, Anthropic says to wait that many seconds, and OpenAI treats it as a minimum and suggests adding a small random delay. Retrying after 0.8 s just produces another 429 and spends request budget.

blocks.question: Your 200 workers retry with `sleep = min(cap, base * 2 ** attempt)`. During an incident, graphs show request spikes every few seconds with silence in between. What is the best fix?
options: Lower base so retries happen sooner
Raise cap so later retries wait longer
Replace the fixed sleep with full jitter: a uniform draw between 0 and that value
Add more workers so the backlog clears faster
blocks.explain: Spikes with silence in between are the signature of synchronized retries. Changing base or cap shifts the spikes but keeps every worker in lockstep. Jitter breaks the synchronization, which is what the AWS post and both providers recommend. More workers make the herd larger.

lessons.title: Caching: skip repeated calls, and reuse repeated prefixes

blocks.md:
The cheapest LLM call is the one you never make. There are two very different caches, and you usually want both:

1. An **application-level response cache**, in your code: if an identical request was answered before, return the stored answer without calling the API.
2. **Provider prompt caching**, on the provider's side: when many requests start with the same long prefix (instructions, tool definitions, a document), the provider reuses its processing of that prefix, so input costs less and the response starts sooner. The model still generates a fresh answer every time.

A response cache needs a **key** that is equal exactly when the answer would be interchangeable. Hash a canonical serialization of every input that changes the output: model, system prompt, messages, temperature and other sampling settings, tools, output schema. Then normalize what does not matter, such as case and whitespace for a classification prompt, so that trivially different requests share a key.

blocks.title: Normalizing before hashing makes two variants share a key

scenes.caption: Request A has prompt "Summarize ticket 17". Normalizing lowercases and collapses whitespace.
Everything that changes the output goes in the payload: model, prompt, sampling settings, output schema. json.dumps with sort_keys gives a stable byte string.
SHA-256 of that string (with schema_id "ticket_summary_v1"). The key for A starts 3b352af977d7.
Request B is "summarize  ticket 17 " (lowercase, double space, trailing space). After normalization the payload is identical, so the key is the same 3b352af977d7: a cache hit.
Putting the raw prompt in the payload instead gives a48d0b9a8d68 for A and 88b3064858ff for B: two misses for the same question. Normalize only what cannot change the answer.

blocks.title: Simulated hit rate: raw keys versus normalized keys

scenes.caption: 10,000 requests over 2,000 distinct questions with Zipf popularity (exponent 1), each written in one of 3 surface variants. Raw keys produce 2,555 distinct entries and a 74.5% hit rate.
Normalizing collapses the variants: 1,443 distinct entries and an 85.6% hit rate. About 44% of the raw-key misses (1,112 of 2,555) were not real misses at all.

blocks.md: Hit rate $h$ drives both cost and latency. A hit costs zero API tokens and takes as long as a cache lookup, $L_h$; a miss costs a full call and takes $L_m$:

blocks.caption: Both are linear in the miss rate 1 - h. Going from 80% to 90% hits halves the API bill and roughly halves the mean latency (0.404 s to 0.2045 s in the example below).

blocks.title: Mean latency versus cache hit rate

scenes.caption: Miss 2.0 s, hit 5 ms (illustrative). At 80% hits the mean is 0.404 s and the cost is 20% of uncached; at 90% it is about 0.20 s and 10%. The last points of hit rate are worth the most.

blocks.md: A response cache freezes one sample. With temperature above zero, the uncached model would give varied answers; the cache always returns the first one. That is usually fine for labeling and extraction, wrong for "generate 5 different ideas". Include anything that should produce a different answer in the key, give entries an expiry, and never cache errors.

**Prompt caching** works on prefixes. Anthropic's version is opt-in with `cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"}` on a content block (or once at the top level for automatic placement); the cached prefix covers tools, then system, then messages, up to that block. Entries have a short default lifetime refreshed on each hit, with a longer option. Usage reports `cache_creation_input_tokens` and `cache_read_input_tokens`. [OpenAI](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching) caches automatically for prompts above a minimum length and reports `cached_tokens`.

Both require an **exact prefix match**: change one character early in the prompt and everything after it misses. Put stable content first and per-request content (the ticket, a timestamp) last.

Pricing details change, but the shape is stable: a cache **write** can cost somewhat more than normal input and a cache **read** costs much less. The plot uses a 3,000-token shared prefix and a 200-token per-request suffix. Plug in your provider's current multipliers; the defaults are illustrative.

blocks.title: Prompt caching: input cost relative to no caching

scenes.caption: One request alone pays the write premium: 1.234x. Two requests already cost 0.695x, ten cost 0.264x, fifty 0.178x. Caching pays off when the prefix is reused within its lifetime.
A short prefix relative to the suffix leaves little to save. Caching helps most for long shared instructions or documents.

blocks.md: On Anthropic, cache reads also help with rate limits: the docs say that for most current models only uncached input tokens count toward ITPM, so a high cache hit rate raises effective input throughput without a limit increase.

blocks.question: You put the current timestamp at the top of the system prompt "for context", followed by 4,000 tokens of fixed instructions, and mark the instructions for prompt caching. Cache reads stay at zero. Why?
options: Timestamps are filtered out before caching
The prefix differs on every request because it starts with a new timestamp, so no request ever matches a previous prefix exactly
Prompt caching only works for the messages part, not the system prompt
The cache needs at least 10 identical requests before it activates
blocks.explain: Prompt caching matches exact prefixes from the start of the request. Anything that varies, placed before the cached content, makes every prefix unique. Anthropic's docs warn about this trap: content that changes every request, such as a timestamp, must not sit inside the cached prefix. Move the timestamp after the cached block, at the end of the prompt.

blocks.question: Your response cache hit rate rises from 80% to 90%. Misses take 2 s and cost 1 unit; hits take 5 ms and are free. What happens to API cost and mean latency?
options: Both drop by about 10%
Cost halves but latency barely changes
Latency halves but cost barely changes
Both roughly halve: cost from 0.2 to 0.1 units per request, latency from about 0.40 s to about 0.20 s
blocks.explain: Both are proportional to the miss rate, which falls from 0.2 to 0.1. Cost per request goes 0.2 to 0.1 units; mean latency goes 0.8 x 0.005 + 0.2 x 2 = 0.404 s to 0.9 x 0.005 + 0.1 x 2 = 0.2045 s.

lessons.title: Batch jobs, idempotent pipelines and putting it together

blocks.md:
Many LLM workloads do not need an answer within seconds: nightly labeling, evaluations, backfilling embeddings or summaries. For those, both providers offer an **asynchronous batch** interface: Anthropic's **Message Batches API** and OpenAI's **Batch API**. You submit many requests at once, the provider processes them on its own schedule, and you collect results later.

The trade is latency for cost and throughput. Both providers price batch requests well below real-time calls (see their current pricing pages) and give batches their own rate-limit pool, so a big backfill does not starve your interactive traffic.

The shape is the same on both. Every request carries a **custom_id** you choose. Anthropic says most batches finish in less than an hour and results become available when all requests are done or after 24 hours, whichever comes first; requests not processed in that window **expire** and are not billed. OpenAI uses a JSONL input file and a 24-hour completion window. Both warn that **results can come back in any order**, so you must match them by custom_id.

blocks.title: An asynchronous batch job, end to end

scenes.caption: Build one request per item, each with a unique custom_id (here the ticket id). Submit them together in one call.
The API returns a batch id immediately with status in_progress. Save the id before doing anything else, so a crash cannot make you submit the same batch twice.
Poll at a relaxed interval. Most batches finish well within the maximum window, but no individual result is guaranteed sooner.
Stream the results. They can arrive in any order, so join on custom_id, never on position. Each result is succeeded, errored, canceled or expired.
Upsert each result keyed by custom_id, and resubmit only errored or expired ones in a new batch. Re-running the whole job writes the same rows again instead of duplicating them.

blocks.md: Prompt caching and batches combine, but Anthropic notes that batch requests are processed concurrently and in any order, so cache hits are best effort, and suggests the longer cache lifetime because a batch can take longer than the default lifetime.

Real pipelines crash halfway and get re-run, and retries mean a request may be sent more than once. A step is **idempotent** if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. RFC 9110 uses this to decide what can be retried automatically: PUT, DELETE and safe methods are idempotent, while a client "SHOULD NOT automatically retry" a non-idempotent request unless it knows the request is actually idempotent.

An LLM generation call is a POST, but it changes nothing on the provider except your bill. Retrying it costs money and may give a different answer; it does not corrupt anything. The danger is in **your side effects**: inserting a row, sending an email, charging a card, calling a tool.

Make side effects idempotent with a stable key per logical operation: the custom_id, the cache key, or a ticket id plus a step name.

- Write results with an **upsert** keyed by that id, not an insert.
- Record the batch id or "done" marker before moving on, and check it on restart.
- For external APIs that support it, pass an **idempotency key**. Stripe's docs describe the pattern: the server saves the result of the first request with a given key and returns it for retries, and errors if the parameters differ.

blocks.title: One request through a well-behaved client

scenes.caption: Hit path: the item is normalized and hashed, the key is found in the cache, and the answer returns in milliseconds without touching any limit.
Miss path: if an identical request is already in flight, wait for it instead of sending a duplicate. Otherwise take a semaphore permit and a rate-limit token before calling the API.
Throttled: a 429 or 5xx goes to the retry step, which waits (Retry-After or jittered backoff) and must get a new token before trying again.
Success: store the answer under its key (never store errors), then return it. The next identical item will take the hit path.

blocks.md: Order of checks for each call: cache first (free, instant), then dedupe in-flight duplicates, then a concurrency limit and a rate limiter, then the API with bounded jittered retries. Anything that is not latency-sensitive goes to a batch job. Every side effect is keyed so that re-running the job is safe.

blocks.question: You must classify 2 million archived documents by next week, and your interactive product shares the same API account. Which plan fits best?
options: A batch job with a custom_id per document, results upserted by custom_id
Real-time calls with a semaphore of 500 and aggressive retries
Real-time calls one at a time to stay under the limits
Real-time calls with temperature 0 so the response cache absorbs most of the load
blocks.explain: Nothing here needs an answer in seconds. Batches cost less, run on a separate rate-limit pool so the product keeps its real-time capacity, and custom_id plus upserts make partial failures and re-runs safe. A huge semaphore competes with your own product for the shared limit, and distinct documents give the response cache nothing to reuse.

blocks.question: Your worker calls the LLM to draft a reply, then inserts the draft into `replies` and emails the customer. A timeout after the email triggers a retry of the whole step. What is the bug and the fix?
options: No bug, because LLM calls are idempotent
The retry inserts a second row and sends a second email; key the step by ticket id, upsert the row, and record that the email was sent before retrying
The retry should use a higher temperature to avoid duplicate drafts
The timeout should be removed so the step never retries
blocks.explain: Generating twice only wastes tokens, but the insert and the email are non-idempotent side effects that happen again. Keying by ticket id with an upsert and a sent marker (or an idempotency key at the email provider) makes the retry harmless. Removing timeouts trades duplicates for hung workers.

blocks.question: After a crash, your batch script restarts and immediately submits a new batch for all items. What risk did it create, and what prevents it?
options: None; the provider deduplicates batches automatically
Results of the old batch will overwrite the new one
If the first batch was already submitted, every item is processed and billed twice; persist the batch id right after creation and resume polling it on restart
The new batch will be rejected because custom_ids must be globally unique
blocks.explain: Nothing in the docs says batches are deduplicated across submissions; custom_id only needs to be unique within a batch. Saving the batch id before polling makes the submission step idempotent: on restart, look up the stored id and resume.
